paragraphs.heading: What counts as tropical
paragraphs.text: The Köppen climate classification is the most widely used way of sorting the world's climates. In it, tropical climates form group A, the first of five major groups. The rule is about warmth: even the coolest month must average 18 °C (64 °F) or more. A place must also fail the tests for the dry B group before it is counted as tropical.

paragraphs.heading: Where they are and how they feel
paragraphs.text: Group A places mostly lie in the tropics, below 23.5 degrees of latitude north and south. They include lands around the Equator, Central America, north-central South America, central Africa, southern Asia, parts of northern Australia and Pacific islands. Heat and humidity last all year, the sunlight is intense, and temperatures change very little from season to season. There are normally just two seasons, a wet one and a dry one, and how long each lasts depends on the location.

paragraphs.heading: Three types, split by the driest month
paragraphs.text: Group A has three basic types: tropical rainforest (Af), tropical monsoon (Am), and tropical savanna, also called tropical wet and dry (Aw when winters are dry, As when summers are dry). What separates them is the rain in the driest month, written P_dry. A rainforest climate needs a P_dry of at least 60 mm (2.4 in). A monsoon climate falls between 60 mm and the value 100 − (mean annual precipitation in mm)/25, and a savanna climate falls below that value.

paragraphs.heading: The rainforest climate
paragraphs.text: Köppen's Af zone takes its f from feucht, the German word for moist, and usually stays within 5 to 10 degrees of the equator. Averaged over a year, temperatures normally sit from 21 to 30 °C (70 to 86 °F). Rain can top 100 inches a year. The seasons are spread evenly through the year, and there is almost no dry spell. The main examples are the upper Amazon basin, the northern Congo basin and the islands of the East Indies.

paragraphs.heading: The monsoon climate
paragraphs.text: The monsoon climate is hot, with little change through the year and plenty of rain, but it has a short dry season that almost always falls in winter. It is common in south and southeast Asian countries between 10 degrees north and the Tropic of Cancer, and also appears in West Africa and South America. Its average yearly temperature is around 27.05 °C (80.69 °F), with a yearly range of about 3.6 °C (6 °F). Its rain is uneven across the year, and it has three main seasons: cool and dry from fall to late winter, hot and dry in spring, and the rainy monsoon near or during summer.

paragraphs.heading: Plants that never stop growing
paragraphs.text: With so much heat and rain, much of the plant life keeps growing all year round. In many tropical places the plants form layers, with shrubs beneath tall trees, bushes beneath the shrubs and grasses beneath the bushes. The rainforest climate has more kinds of trees than the other tropical types thanks to its rain, and those trees add moisture back to the air through transpiration, the evaporation of water from the surfaces of living plants. Tropical plants also give people valuable crops such as coffee, cocoa and oil palm.
